newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya sees no hurry to reform telecoms.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sees no hurry to reform telecoms.

text.p: Kenya said on Wednesday that a cost-saving satellite system the United Nations wants to install at its Nairobi headquarters to cut costs would start operations only after Kenya's planned telecommunications reforms.

Public Works and Housing Minister Jonathan Ng'eno said neither the United Nations nor any Western country could force Kenya to hasten reform of the telecommunications sector because it involved "sensitive matters of national interest".

Reform would begin in earnest when a new bill to split Kenya Posts & Telecommunications Corp into mail and telecommunications arms and to establish a regulatory authority was presented for debate by parliament, probably in the last quarter of the year.
"After that, any company that wants may come in. We are doing this at our pace, we are not rushing," Ng'eno told a news conference at U.N. headquarters on the outskirts of Nairobi.
The U.N. Centre for Human Settlements (Habitat) and the U.N. Environment Programme have repeatedly asked for installation of the system to help cut costs in line with demands by donors.
Nairobi-based UNEP and Kenya have in principle agreed the system can be installed but bureaucratic and legal delays have impeded any further progress, according to senior U.N. sources.

"There is no time frame in which we expect the U.N. system to be able to install the satellite," Ng'eno told reporters. "We do not liberalise (any sector) to meet the interests of other people. This is a matter of sensitive national interest.
"We understand the few problems with Habitat and the U.N. system. We would like to help as quickly as possible but there are many issues to look at," Ng'eno said.

Habitat and UNEP officials say Kenya's reluctance was based on fears the new system would hit the state-owned KP&TC, which receives $5 million annually from the U.N.'s Nairobi headquarters in phone charges.
